Why MAST and pseudobulk DESeq2 return distinct sets of differentially expressed genes

Source: vignettes/differential_analyses.qmd

1 Why MAST and pseudobulk DESeq2 return near-disjoint DEG sets

The MAST and pseudobulk DESeq2 workflows in scripts/06_02_MAST_biological_exploration_transcriptomic_differential_analyses.R and scripts/06_02_deseq2_biological_exploration_transcriptomic_differential_analyses.R test the same morphotype contrast but define different experimental units, inputs, and likelihoods (Table 1). The sections below explain why they return largely non-overlapping differentially expressed gene (DEG) sets, as summarised in the Venn comparison (scripts/06_02_compare_DEGs.R).

1.1 Notation and indices

Both frameworks are fitted per Luque cell type \(t\), but they define different experimental units and responses (Table 2). All equations below use this shared notation.

Counts are first aggregated within each cell type and organoid:

\[ K_{gst} = \sum_{i \in (s,t)} k_{gi} \tag{1}\]

DESeq2 then models \(K_{gst}\); MAST models \(Y_{gi}\) and \(z_{gi}\) directly and does not use Equation 1.

1.2 The fundamental mismatch: statistical unit of inference

The root cause is that the two frameworks define the experimental unit differently (Table 1, Table 3, Table 2).

Crowell et al. term this the distinction between cell-level and sample-level inference. They write explicitly:

“Most current scRNA-seq differential expression methods are designed to test one set of cells against another … In such statistical models, the cells are the experimental units … [but] the goal shifts to making sample-level inferences (i.e., experimental units are samples), in order to account for sample-to-sample as well as cell-to-cell variability.”

The MAST hurdle model fitted per cell type \(t\) is:

\[ \underbrace{\text{logit}\,P(Y_{gi} > 0)}_{\text{discrete (D)}} = \alpha_g^D + \beta_{g,\mathrm{Morph}}^D\,x_i + \beta_{g,\mathrm{cdr}}^D\,\text{cngeneson}_i \tag{2}\]

\[ \underbrace{E[Y_{gi} \mid Y_{gi} > 0]}_{\text{continuous (C)}} = \alpha_g^C + \beta_{g,\mathrm{Morph}}^C\,x_i + \beta_{g,\mathrm{cdr}}^C\,\text{cngeneson}_i \tag{3}\]

where \(i\) indexes cells (~7,479 for neural). No random effect for Sample.barcode is included (formula = ~ Morphotype + cngeneson, method = "glm"). Cells from the same organoid are therefore treated as independent biological replicates — a form of pseudoreplication.

The DESeq2 model works on Equation 1 and tests:

\[ K_{gst} \sim \text{NB}(\mu_{gst},\,\phi_g), \quad \log\mu_{gst} = \beta_{g0t} + \beta_{gt,\mathrm{Morph}}\,x_s + \log S_{st} \tag{4}\]

where \(s\) indexes organoids (12 per group). The likelihood-ratio test (LRT) compares \(\sim\text{Morphotype}\) vs \(\sim 1\), with \(\sim 22\) effective degrees of freedom.

Together, Equation 2, Equation 3, and Equation 4 formalise the core design difference: MAST conditions on cell-level covariates and treats cells as replicates, whereas DESeq2 models organoid-level count variation after pseudobulk aggregation.

1.3 Artificial inflation of statistical power in MAST

The hurdle LRT statistic is:

\[ \Lambda = 2\bigl[\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{full}}) - \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{reduced}})\bigr] \xrightarrow{H_0} \chi^2_1 \tag{5}\]

Under standard regression, power scales with \(\sqrt{n}\). When \(n = n_{\text{cells}} \approx 7{,}479\) rather than \(n = n_{\text{samples}} = 24\), the effective standard error of \(\hat\beta_{g,\mathrm{Morph}}\) shrinks by roughly \(\sqrt{7{,}479 / 24} \approx 18\)-fold. Biological noise shared across cells within the same organoid is treated as independent signal, inflating \(\Lambda\) in Equation 5 and producing very small p-values for effects invisible with sample-level replication. Crowell et al. demonstrate (Fig. 3):

“Most isolated intersections, i.e., hits unique to a certain method, were genes that had been stimulated to be EE [equally expressed] and thus false discoveries … AD, MAST, and scDD methods report large numbers of isolated hits”

The Venn results are consistent with this: MAST returns 41 FDR-significant DEGs in neural cells; DESeq2 returns 0. The 41 MAST-specific hits match the expected pattern of inflated false positives from pseudoreplication.

1.4 Why DESeq2 returns no FDR-significant DEGs after correction

With 12 vs 12 organoids and \(m \approx 11{,}352\) tested genes, the Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) threshold for the \(k\)-th ranked p-value is:

\[ p_{(k)} \leq \frac{k}{m}\,q = \frac{k}{11{,}352} \times 0.05 \tag{6}\]

The data show 575 genes with raw \(p < 0.05\) in neural, but the minimum adjusted p-value is 0.133. The raw p-value distribution is only weakly enriched below 0.05 — consistent with a real but weak signal below the power resolution of 12 biological replicates. For a gene to survive BH at position \(k = 1\), Equation 6 requires:

\[ p_{\min} \leq \frac{1}{11{,}352} \times 0.05 \approx 4.4 \times 10^{-6} \tag{7}\]

The observed minimum raw p-value is \(\approx 9.8 \times 10^{-6}\), just above the bound in Equation 7. DESeq2 is not failing to detect biology; it correctly acknowledges that 12 organoids cannot separate signal from noise at genome-wide FDR 5% given the effect sizes present.

1.5 Different model assumptions and input data

Beyond replication, the likelihoods, input scale, and covariate handling summarised in Table 1 are formalised below. The cngeneson covariate absorbs sequencing-depth variation at the cell level:

\[ \text{cngeneson}_i = \frac{\text{n\_detected}_i - \overline{\text{n\_detected}}}{\text{SD}(\text{n\_detected})} \tag{8}\]

If cells from neural_bias organoids have systematically higher CDR, its coefficient in Equation 2 and Equation 3 may absorb transcriptome-wide morphotype differences, or partially remove capture-efficiency confounding. DESeq2 handles depth through \(S_{st}\) in Equation 4 at the pseudobulk level only.

MAST therefore models detection and expression on a log-normalised, cell-level scale, whereas DESeq2 models count overdispersion after Equation 1. Crowell et al. (Supplementary Fig. 5) show that hurdle and mixed models on log counts systematically underestimate logFCs compared with NB pseudobulk methods on raw counts.

1.6 Resolution of biological signal

The statistical differences above also explain why downstream enrichment profiles diverge between frameworks.

DESeq2 captures organoid-level developmental programs. Pseudobulk aggregation averages over cells within each \((s,t)\) stratum:

\[ \bar{q}_{gt}^{(s)} = \frac{1}{n_{st}} \sum_{i \in (s,t)} q_{gi} \tag{9}\]

Cell-to-cell stochasticity is suppressed; a pathway becomes significant only when many genes shift coherently across organoids. This favours axial/regionalisation programs, morphogen-response modules, and stable cell-type regulatory states. Accordingly, DESeq2 enrichment emphasises neural regionalisation and somitic FGFR signalling — large-scale tissue-patterning programs consistent with axial organisation in the Villaronga-Luque gastruloid model.

MAST captures fine-grained metabolic and signalling heterogeneity. Via Equation 2, MAST can detect shifts in

\[ P(Y_{gi} > 0 \mid \text{neural\_bias}) \neq P(Y_{gi} > 0 \mid \text{TLS}) \]

even when Equation 9 changes only weakly. It is sensitive to subpopulations with stronger OXPHOS, somitic glucose/glycolysis activation, NMP gap-junction turnover, and small retinoic-acid or junctional substates. MAST enrichment accordingly highlights OXPHOS/electron transport, glucose metabolism, gap junctions, cadherin/adherens signalling, and retinoic acid — differences that may affect only a fraction of cells and are diluted by Equation 1.

These biological contrasts are real hypotheses, but MAST-specific enrichment must be weighed against the pseudoreplication caveat in Section 1.3: without a (1 \mid \text{Sample.barcode}) random effect, thousands of dependent cells inflate significance.

1.7 Summary of contributing causes, ranked by importance

  1. Pseudoreplication (dominant effect). MAST without a (1 \mid \text{Sample.barcode}) random effect treats \(n \approx 7{,}500\) dependent cells as independent replicates, inflating the LRT in Equation 5 by a factor of \(\sim n_{\text{cells}}/n_{\text{samples}} \approx 300\). This alone explains the large number of MAST-specific hits and the lack of overlap with DESeq2.

  2. Low biological replication in DESeq2. With 12 organoids per group and ~11,000 genes, DESeq2 is correctly conservative: 575 genes pass raw \(p < 0.05\), but none survive Equation 6. The minimum padj of 0.133 is the honest answer given the data.

  3. Different resolution of biological signal. Equation 9 and Equation 4 favour organoid-coherent patterning programs; Equation 2 and Equation 3 favour cell-state heterogeneity (Section 1.6).

  4. Different likelihoods and input data. As in Table 1, MAST’s hurdle GLM on log-normalised data and DESeq2’s NB model on raw counts capture different aspects of expression variability. LFCs are not on the same scale and are not expected to rank genes identically.

  5. cngeneson covariate. MAST regresses out cellular CDR via Equation 8, modifying which genes appear significant relative to DESeq2.

1.8 Interpretation and integrated biological model

Statistical caution. MAST results reflect largely cell-level variation without organoid-to-organoid variability and should be treated cautiously. The replication-aware estimate is DESeq2’s: effect sizes are below what 12 organoids can resolve at genome-wide FDR (Equation 6, Equation 7). The raw-\(p\) overlap in the Venn comparison (4 genes at sample level, 3–4 at cell-type level) is the most credible shared set.

Integrated biological model. The frameworks are nonetheless compatible with the Villaronga-Luque model of early metabolic bias in NMPs shaping the fate landscape:

  1. Original paper: higher glycolysis supports TLS formation and mesodermal/somitic output; lower glycolysis and/or compensatory OXPHOS associates with neural-biased outcomes.
  2. DESeq2 (120 h): early differences manifest as organoid-level programs. TLS retains stronger neural regionalisation and somitic FGFR signalling, consistent with better axial and paraxial-mesoderm patterning.
  3. MAST (120 h): the same phenotype decomposes into finer cell states — neural OXPHOS/electron transport, somitic glucose/glycolysis, and junctional or retinoic-acid substates in NMP, pluripotent, and unknown compartments.

Pseudo-bulk DESeq2 recovers the tissue-level transcriptional consequences of morphotype divergence — regionalisation and FGFR-associated somitic organisation — whereas MAST resolves cell-state metabolic and signalling heterogeneity, especially OXPHOS, glucose metabolism, and cell-cell communication. Both are compatible with metabolic imbalance preceding, and likely helping drive, the neural-biased versus TLS-like phenotypic landscape.

To increase DESeq2 power, options include more biological replicates or a model that borrows strength across cell types (e.g. muscat with its pbDS wrapper around edgeR/DESeq2 using shared dispersion).
